exampleAnswers.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find \begin{align*} 2 \cdot 8^{2x} & \lt \dfrac{1}{3} \\[5pt] 8^{2x} & \lt \dfrac{1}{6}. \end{align*}

Then, taking the logarithm to base $8$ of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get \begin{align*} \log_8 \left( 8^{2x} \right) &\lt \log_8 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right) \\[5pt] 2x &\lt \log_8 \left( 6^{-1} \right) \\[5pt] 2x &\lt -\log_8 \left( 6 \right) \\[5pt] x &\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\lt} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{- \dfrac{1}{2} \log_8 \left( 6 \right)}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 4^{x} &\gt 7 \\[5pt] 4^{x} &\gt 14. \end{align*}

Then, taking the logarithm to base $4$ of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get \begin{align*} \log_4 \left( 4^{x} \right) &\gt \log_4 \left( 14 \right) \\[5pt] x &\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\gt} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ \log_4 \left( 14 \right)}. \end{align*}

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

\[\begin{align*} 3e^x - 4 &< 0 \\[5pt] 3e^x &< 4 \\[5pt] e^x &< \dfrac{4}{3}. \\[5pt] \end{align*}\]

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

\[\begin{align*} \ln \left( e^x \right) &< \ln \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right) \\[5pt] x &< \ln 4 - \ln 3 . \\[5pt] \end{align*}\]

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find \begin{align*} \dfrac{3e^x-e^{3/2}}{2\sqrt{e}} &\gt e \\[5pt] 3e^x-e^{3/2} &\gt 2e\sqrt{e} \\[5pt] 3e^x-e^{3/2} &\gt 2e \cdot e^{1/2} \\[5pt] 3e^x-e^{3/2} &\gt 2e^{(1+\frac{1}{2})} \\[5pt] 3e^x-e^{3/2} &\gt 2e^{3/2} \\[5pt] 3e^x &\gt 3e^{3/2} \\[5pt] e^x &\gt e^{3/2}. \end{align*}

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get \begin{align*} \ln (e^x) &\gt \ln(e^{3/2}) \\[5pt] x &\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\gt} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ \dfrac{3}{2}}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find \begin{align*} 4\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{x-1} - 8 & \leq 0\\[5pt] 4\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{x-1} & \leq 8\\[5pt] \left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{x-1} & \leq 2. \end{align*}

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get \begin{align*} \ln \left[ \left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{x-1} \right] & \leq \ln{2} \\[5pt] (x-1) \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right) & \leq \ln{2}\\[5pt] (x-1) \left(\ln{2} - \ln{7} \right) & \leq \ln{2}. \end{align*}

Lastly, note that $\ln{2}-\ln{7}$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality: \begin{align*} x - 1 & \geq \dfrac{\ln{2}}{\ln{2} - \ln{7}}\\[5pt] x & \geq \dfrac{\ln{2}}{\ln{2} - \ln{7}} + 1 \end{align*}

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find \begin{align*} 3e - \dfrac{1}{2} \left( 0.99 \right)^x &\gt -2e \\[5pt] -\dfrac{1}{2} \left( 0.99 \right)^x &\gt -5e \\[5pt] \left( 0.99 \right)^x &\lt 10e. \end{align*}

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get \begin{align*} \ln \left[ (0.99)^{x} \right] &\lt \ln (10e) \\[5pt] x \ln (0.99) &\lt \ln (10e) \end{align*}

Lastly, note that $\ln (0.99)$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality: \begin{align*} x &\gt \dfrac{\ln (10e)}{\ln (0.99)} \end{align*}

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

\[\begin{align*} 5 \cdot \left( \dfrac{4}{9} \right)^x &< 25 \\[5pt] \left( \dfrac{4}{9} \right)^x &< 5 . \end{align*}\]

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

\[\begin{align*} \ln \left[ \left( \dfrac{4}{9} \right)^x \right] &< \ln 5 \\[5pt] x \ln \left( \dfrac{4}{9} \right) &< \ln 5 \\[5pt] x \left( \ln 4 - \ln 9 \right) &< \ln 5. \end{align*}\]

Lastly, note that $\ln 4 - \ln 9$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

\[\begin{align*} x &> \dfrac{\ln 5}{\ln 4 - \ln 9} \\[5pt] \end{align*}\]

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x+1} & \leq \dfrac{1}{9}\\[5pt] \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x+1} & \leq \dfrac{1}{3}. \end{align*}

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get \begin{align*} \ln \left[ \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x+1} \right] & \leq \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\[5pt] (x+1) \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) & \leq \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\\[5pt] (x+1) \left(\ln{1} - \ln{2} \right) & \leq \ln{1} - \ln{3}\\[5pt] (x+1) \left(-\ln{2} \right) & \leq -\ln{3}. \end{align*}

Lastly, note that $-\ln{2}$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality: \begin{align*} x + 1 & \geq \dfrac{-\ln{3}}{-\ln{2}}\\[5pt] x & \geq \dfrac{\ln{3}}{\ln{2}} - 1 \end{align*}

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One

question.explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

\[\begin{align*} \left( 0.45 \right)^{x+3} - 10 &\geq 0 \\[5pt] \left( 0.45 \right)^{x+3} &\geq 10 . \end{align*}\]

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

\[\begin{align*} \ln \left[ (0.45)^{x+3} \right] &\geq \ln (10) \\[5pt] (x+3) \ln (0.45) &\geq \ln (10) \end{align*}\]

Lastly, note that $\ln (0.45)$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

\[\begin{align*} x+3 &\leq \dfrac{\ln (10)}{\ln (0.45)} \\[5pt] x &\leq \dfrac{\ln (10)}{\ln (0.45)} -3 \\[5pt] \end{align*}\]

exampleAnswers.title: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number

question.explanation:
First, we isolate the exponential term: \begin{align*} -4 - e^{3x} &> 2 \\[5pt] -e^{3x} &> 6 \\[5pt] e^{3x} &< -6. \end{align*}

Next, recall that a positive number raised to any real power is always positive. Since $e > 0,$ we have \[ e^{3x} > 0 \] for every real value of $x.$

Therefore, $e^{3x}$ cannot be less than $-6.$ Hence, the inequality \[ e^{3x} < -6 \] has no solutions.

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number

question.explanation:
First, we isolate the exponential term: \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 7^{3x - 1} + 1 &> 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 7^{3x - 1} &> -1 \\[5pt] 7^{3x - 1} &> -2. \end{align*}

Next, recall that a positive number raised to any real power is always positive. Since $7 > 0,$ we have \[ 7^{3x - 1} > 0 \] for every real value of $x.$

In particular, every value of $7^{3x - 1}$ is greater than $-2.$ Therefore, \[ 7^{3x - 1} > -2 \] for all real values of $x.$

Hence, the original inequality is satisfied for all real numbers.

example.title: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number

question.explanation:
First, we isolate the exponential term: \begin{align*} \dfrac{3}{2}(0.43)^{4x + 5} + 4 &> -2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{3}{2}(0.43)^{4x + 5} &> -6 \\[5pt] (0.43)^{4x + 5} &> -4. \end{align*}

Next, recall that a positive number raised to any real power is always positive. Since $0.43 > 0,$ we have \[ (0.43)^{4x + 5} > 0 \] for every real value of $x.$

In particular, every value of $(0.43)^{4x + 5}$ is greater than $-4.$ Therefore, \[ (0.43)^{4x + 5} > -4 \] for all real values of $x.$

Hence, the original inequality is satisfied for all real numbers.

question.explanation: Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following: \begin{align*} 7^{x+1} & \gt 5^{x-1}\\[5pt] \ln\left( 7^{x+1} \right) & \gt \ln\left( 5^{x-1} \right) \\[5pt] (x+1)\ln{7} & \gt (x-1)\ln{5}\\[5pt] x\ln{7} + \ln{7} & \gt x\ln{5} - \ln{5}\\[5pt] x\ln{7} - x\ln{5} & \gt -\ln{5} - \ln{7}\\[5pt] x(\ln{7} - \ln{5}) & \gt -\ln{5} - \ln{7}\\[5pt] x & \gt -\dfrac{\ln{5} + \ln{7}}{\ln{7} - \ln{5}}\\[5pt] x & \gt \dfrac{\ln{5} + \ln{7}}{\ln{5} - \ln{7}} \end{align*}

example.title: Solving an Inequality with Exponential Functions on Both Sides

question.explanation:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following: \begin{align*} 3\cdot 2^{1-3x} & \ge \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x-4}\\[5pt] \ln\left( 3\cdot 2^{1-3x} \right) & \ge \ln\left[ \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x-4} \right] \\[5pt] \ln{3} + (1-3x)\ln{2} & \ge (x-4)\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\\[5pt] \ln{3} + (1-3x)\ln{2} & \ge (x-4)(\ln{1} - \ln{3})\\[5pt] \ln{3} + (1-3x)\ln{2} & \ge (x-4)(0 - \ln{3})\\[5pt] \ln{3} + (1-3x)\ln{2} & \ge (4-x)\ln{3}\\[5pt] \ln{3} + \ln{2} - 3x\ln{2} & \ge 4\ln{3} - x\ln{3}\\[5pt] x\ln{3} - 3x\ln{2} & \ge 4\ln{3} - \ln{3} - \ln{2}\\[5pt] x(\ln{3} - 3\ln{2}) & \ge 3\ln{3} - \ln{2} \end{align*}

Notice that $\ln 3 - 3\ln 2 = \ln 3 - \ln 8.$ Since $3 < 8,$ we know that $\ln 3 < \ln 8.$ Therefore, $\ln 3 - \ln 8 < 0.$ Because we are dividing both sides of the inequality by a negative number, we must reverse the direction of the inequality sign: \[ x \le \dfrac{3\ln{3} - \ln{2}}{\ln{3} - 3\ln{2}} \]
